analogy.p: Natural conception is like a gardener who waits for one seed to sprout in the soil. Fertility drugs are like fertiliser that helps seeds that would not otherwise grow to sprout. IVF is like growing several seedlings in a greenhouse tray (the laboratory dish) and then planting the best one or two back into the garden bed (the uterus). Planting too many seedlings crowds the bed, just as too many embryos risks multiple births. The analogy breaks down because there is no guarantee that a planted embryo will implant, and ethical questions about embryos have no real equivalent for seedlings.
analogy.t: A garden with a difficult seed bed

bullets: **Infertility** = unable to reproduce naturally; this topic is **Higher tier (HT) only**.
Eggs only mature and are released if the pituitary releases enough **FSH** and **LH** at the right times.
If a woman does not produce enough **FSH**, her eggs do not mature, so she cannot conceive naturally.
Treatments either **boost the woman's own hormones** (fertility drugs) or **bypass natural fertilisation** (IVF).
Hormone treatments are examples of using knowledge of **negative feedback** and the menstrual cycle in medicine.
Both partners can be infertile; the spec mainly covers treatments aimed at the female partner.
Success of any treatment is measured as a **live birth rate**, not just a pregnancy.
core.h: What infertility is and why hormones can treat it
core.p: **Infertility** is the inability to conceive naturally, or to have a baby, despite regular unprotected intercourse. It has many causes in both sexes, including problems with the hormones that control egg and sperm production, blocked oviducts, and low sperm numbers. The spec focuses on hormonal causes in women and on treatments that use hormones. Because the menstrual cycle is controlled by hormones from the pituitary, a woman whose pituitary does not make enough of the right hormone may not mature or release eggs. Giving the missing hormone as a drug can then restore ovulation, which is why this topic builds directly on the menstrual cycle.

bullets: The spec: 'FSH and LH can be given in a **fertility drug** to a woman whose own level of FSH is too low to stimulate eggs to mature'.
**FSH** matures the egg in the ovary (and stimulates oestrogen production).
**LH** stimulates the release of the egg (ovulation).
The woman can then **conceive naturally**; no laboratory fertilisation is needed with this treatment alone.
Risk: **multiple eggs** may be released, so there is a chance of **twins or triplets**.
The hormones are given by **injection** as they would be digested if swallowed (they are proteins).
This works because the **target organ** (ovary) still responds; it will not help if the ovaries or oviducts are damaged.
Link to contraception: the pill does the opposite, **inhibiting** FSH to prevent egg maturation.
core.p: The first treatment in the spec is the use of **FSH and LH** as **fertility drugs**. If a woman's own level of FSH is too low to stimulate her eggs to mature, she can be given FSH and LH by injection. **FSH** causes an egg to mature in the ovary (and the follicle to produce oestrogen), and **LH** stimulates the release of the egg (ovulation). This copies the natural cycle, so the woman may then ovulate and conceive naturally by intercourse. The drugs are given as hormones, so they travel in the blood to the target organ, the ovary. A drawback is that the ovary may respond too strongly and release **more than one egg**.

bullets: **IVF = in vitro fertilisation**: fertilisation happens in the laboratory.
Used when other treatments have not worked, or the egg and sperm cannot meet naturally.
Hormones (FSH and LH) are used to control and boost egg production.
The father's **sperm** is used (or donor sperm) to fertilise the eggs.
Embryos are placed in the **uterus** so they can implant in the lining.
A baby born by IVF develops normally after implantation; the difference is only how fertilisation happens.
IVF requires specialist clinics, which is why it is expensive and not available to everyone through the NHS.
core.h: IVF: what it is and when it is used
core.p: **IVF** stands for **in vitro fertilisation**, meaning fertilisation 'in glass', that is, in a laboratory dish rather than inside the body. It is used when other treatments have failed, for example when the oviducts are blocked, so that sperm and egg cannot meet naturally. In IVF hormones are used to stimulate the ovaries to mature several eggs at once, the eggs are collected, fertilised outside the body, allowed to start developing, and then one or two embryos are put back into the uterus so that pregnancy can continue naturally. Understanding both the order of events and the reason for each step is what wins marks.

bullets: **Step 1**: the mother is given **FSH and LH** to stimulate the maturation of **several eggs**.
**Step 2**: the **eggs are collected** from the mother's ovaries.
**Step 3**: the eggs are **fertilised by the father's sperm in the laboratory**.
**Step 4**: the fertilised eggs **develop into embryos** (tiny balls of cells).
**Step 5**: at this stage **one or two embryos are inserted into the mother's uterus** (womb).
Why several eggs? Not every egg fertilises or develops into a healthy embryo, so more eggs give a better chance.
Why only one or two embryos? Transferring too many increases the chance of **multiple pregnancy** and its risks.
Surplus embryos may be frozen, donated to research or destroyed, which raises ethical questions.
core.h: The stages of IVF in order
core.p: Learn IVF as five stages in strict order, with the hormone and the reason at each stage. First the mother is given **FSH and LH** to stimulate the maturation of **several eggs** (more than the one egg of a normal cycle). The eggs are then **collected** from the mother using a fine needle through the vagina wall. They are **fertilised in the laboratory** with sperm from the father. The fertilised eggs develop into **embryos**, which are observed until they are **tiny balls of cells**. Finally **one or two embryos** are inserted into the mother's uterus, where hopefully one implants into the lining and develops into a fetus.

bullets: **FSH** given to cause **several eggs to mature** in the ovary.
**LH** given to stimulate **release** (ovulation) at the right time.
This gives a bigger collection of eggs, increasing the chance of at least one **embryo** forming.
Hormone doses are carefully controlled because too much can cause **ovarian hyperstimulation**, a painful and sometimes dangerous swelling of the ovaries.
Hormones are given by injection and treatment lasts several weeks, which is physically demanding.
Because the mother's own hormone system is manipulated, hormones can have **side effects** such as mood swings, headaches and bloating.
Compare natural cycle (one egg) with IVF cycle (several eggs).
This is a good example of the 'How Science Works' idea that technology can be developed from biological understanding.
core.h: Why hormones are needed in IVF
core.p: In a natural cycle only one egg normally matures. For IVF the doctors want several eggs, so they give extra **FSH**, which causes more than one follicle to mature, and **LH**, which stimulates release (or the eggs are collected just before release). The mother's own natural hormone cycle is also often controlled with other drugs so the timing of egg collection and embryo transfer is predictable. This is an example of **applying biological knowledge**: because FSH matures eggs and LH triggers ovulation, giving them in the right amounts at the right time lets scientists control the process.

bullets: **Success rate** = (number of live births ÷ number of treatment cycles) × 100.
Success **decreases with the woman's age**, especially after about 35.
Many couples need **more than one cycle**, which adds cost and stress.
Success is also affected by the **health of the embryos** and whether they **implant** in the uterus lining.
Statistics can be reported per cycle, per embryo transferred or per woman, so check what the question measures.
When evaluating data, mention **sample size**, whether groups are comparable, and whether the data come from a reliable source.
A low success rate means many couples go through the physical and emotional stress and the cost without a baby.
Overall average success per cycle in the UK is roughly a quarter or less, and much lower for older women.
core.h: Success rates and what affects them
core.p: IVF does not always work. The **success rate** (the percentage of cycles that lead to a live birth) is **not high** overall, and it varies with many factors. The strongest factor is the **age of the woman**: success falls as she gets older because egg quality and quantity fall. Other factors include the cause of infertility, the quality of sperm and embryos, the number of previous attempts and the skill of the clinic. When an exam gives you data on success rates, describe the trend with numbers, compare groups, and suggest reasons, including the limitations of the data such as sample size.

bullets: Gives a **chance of pregnancy** to people who cannot conceive naturally.
Helps couples with **blocked oviducts** or whose eggs and sperm never meet.
Uses the **parents' own egg and sperm** (unless donors are used), so the baby is genetically theirs.
Embryos can be checked for health before transfer, which can allow screening for serious inherited disorders (extension).
Success can be improved by repeating cycles or freezing surplus embryos.
Benefits for **mental wellbeing** and family life if treatment works.
IVF is a good example of a scientific advance with clear social benefits.
core.p: The spec says you must be able to **evaluate** IVF. Start with the benefits. IVF gives a **chance of a baby to couples who could not conceive** in any other way, which for many people is hugely important for their wellbeing and family life. It has helped millions of babies to be born worldwide. It also allows the fertilised eggs to be observed before transfer, and in some cases it makes it possible to treat women with blocked oviducts or low egg production. Benefits are only part of the picture, so you must balance them with the problems on the next page.

bullets: **Emotionally stressful**: repeated cycles, waiting and disappointment.
**Physically stressful**: hormone injections, side effects and egg collection.
**Success rates not high**, so many people have no baby after treatment.
**Multiple births** (twins, triplets) are risky for **mother and babies** (premature birth, low birth weight, complications).
**Cost**: private treatment is expensive; NHS funding is limited and varies by area.
**Ethical issues**: surplus embryos may be discarded or used in research, which some people object to on religious or moral grounds.
**Health risks** of the drugs, e.g. ovarian hyperstimulation.
Possible age limits and who is eligible raise **social and ethical debates**.
core.h: Evaluating IVF: the problems and risks
core.p: The spec names the main drawbacks: IVF is **emotionally and physically stressful**, the **success rates are not high**, and it can lead to **multiple births**, which are a risk to the babies and the mother. The emotional stress comes from the uncertainty and repeated disappointment. Physical stress comes from the hormone injections and egg collection. Multiple births occur when more than one embryo implants, and they increase the chance of premature birth, low birth weight and complications. There are also **ethical issues** and **cost**, which may mean not everyone can get treatment.

bullets: Transferring more embryos **increases** the chance of at least one pregnancy but **also increases** multiple births.
**Multiple births** increase the risk of **premature birth**, **low birth weight** and complications for the mother.
Premature babies may need intensive care and can have long-term health problems.
Transferring a single embryo gives a lower chance per cycle but is much safer.
The embryos are inserted when they are **tiny balls of cells**, early in development, before the cells specialise.
Frozen spare embryos can be used in later cycles if the first transfer fails.
This is an example of a **risk versus benefit** decision, common in 'evaluate' questions.
core.h: Why only one or two embryos are transferred
core.p: A common exam question asks why the number of embryos is limited. Putting back several embryos would raise the chance that **at least one implants**, but it would also raise the chance of **multiple pregnancy**. Multiple pregnancies are more dangerous because the uterus is overstretched and babies are more likely to be born early and underweight, with health problems. So there is a trade-off between **chance of success** and **safety**. The spec says '**one or two embryos**' are inserted, and in the UK regulators limit the number to reduce multiple births.

bullets: **For**: allows couples to have children, so improves wellbeing and family life.
**Against (religious or ethical)**: some people believe that an embryo has the right to life, so discarding embryos is wrong.
**Cost and funding**: should taxpayers fund IVF when money could treat other conditions?
**Access and fairness**: availability depends on location and age limits (the 'postcode lottery').
**Welfare of the child**: concerns about older parents, multiple births and health risks.
**Regulation** by law (in the UK the HFEA) controls licensing, number of embryos and research.
A 6 mark answer should show both sides and reach a justified conclusion.
core.p: Questions often ask you to consider ethical or social views, not just scientific facts. People have different views on IVF because of different **beliefs and values**. Some support it because it helps people to have children and reduces suffering. Others raise concerns about the **status of embryos** (since surplus embryos are discarded or used for research), about **who should pay**, and about **age limits** or whether treatment should be offered to all. In exams, give a balanced view, use the word 'some people' and avoid just stating your own opinion.

bullets: Link: **FSH and LH** have the same roles in IVF as in the natural menstrual cycle.
Link: **contraceptive pill** inhibits FSH; **fertility drugs** supply FSH. Compare these two uses of the same hormone knowledge.
Link: **embryo** development and **implantation** follow the same biology as natural pregnancy.
Link: **stem cell** and **embryo research** raise similar ethical issues.
Exam skill: for '**describe IVF**' write the five stages in order with the hormones named.
Exam skill: for '**evaluate**' use 'however' to contrast pros and cons and conclude.
Exam skill: for data, compare using **percentages** and quote figures with units.
Remember this content is for **Higher tier** (HT) only in Biology, so it appears on the Higher paper only.
core.h: Links to other topics and exam skills
core.p: This topic connects strongly to the **menstrual cycle** (FSH, LH roles), **negative feedback** (the body's own control that the drugs override), **contraception** (the pill inhibits FSH, whereas fertility treatment supplies FSH), and **ethics of scientific developments** (stem cells, genetic screening). To answer well, remember to identify the hormone, its source and its effect, put the IVF stages in order, and in evaluation questions give advantages, disadvantages and a conclusion.

exam: 'Describe IVF' (4 to 6 marks): give all five stages in order: FSH and LH given, eggs collected, fertilised with sperm in laboratory, embryos develop, one or two inserted into uterus.
'State the role of FSH/LH in fertility treatment' (2 marks): FSH matures eggs; LH stimulates release of eggs.
'Evaluate IVF' (4 to 6 marks): at least two advantages and two disadvantages (emotionally and physically stressful, low success rate, multiple births) and a conclusion.
'Suggest why only one or two embryos are put back': to reduce the chance of multiple births, which are risky for mother and babies.
Data questions: quote values with units, calculate the percentage success, compare age groups, and mention sample size as a limitation.
Use 'whereas' or 'however' to show an evaluation, and always finish with a justified judgement.
'Explain why a woman with low FSH is given FSH': FSH stimulates the maturation of an egg in the ovary; without it eggs do not mature.
Link back: 'Compare the pill and fertility drugs': the pill inhibits FSH; fertility drugs supply FSH and LH.
Spellings: infertility, fertilisation, embryo, uterus, ovulation, in vitro.
Ethics questions: use 'some people believe' and give both sides; marks are for reasoning, not for your opinion.

mistakes.r: Only fertilisation and early embryo development happen in the laboratory; embryos are then inserted into the uterus.
mistakes.w: IVF means the baby grows in the laboratory.

mistakes.r: FSH causes maturation of the egg; LH stimulates the release (ovulation).
mistakes.w: FSH releases the egg and LH matures it.

mistakes.r: The mother is given FSH and LH to stimulate several eggs to mature; one or two embryos are inserted.
mistakes.w: Only one egg is used in IVF.

mistakes.r: The success rate is not high, which is one of the disadvantages to include when evaluating.
mistakes.w: IVF has a high success rate.

mistakes.r: Give a reasoned point: stressful, low success, multiple births, ethical issues about embryos.
mistakes.w: IVF is bad because it is unnatural.

mistakes.r: Fertility drugs (FSH and LH) stimulate eggs to mature and be released; the pill is the one that inhibits.
mistakes.w: Fertility drugs stop eggs being released.

mistakes.r: Multiple births are a risk to babies and the mother (premature, low birth weight, complications).
mistakes.w: Multiple births are good because there are more babies.

mistakes.r: Embryos are inserted into the uterus.
mistakes.w: Embryos are put into the oviduct.

summary: The spec (Higher tier only) asks you to understand how hormones are used to treat infertility: FSH and LH given as fertility drugs to women with too little FSH, and IVF, in which hormones stimulate several eggs to mature, the eggs are fertilised in a laboratory and one or two embryos are placed in the uterus. You must also evaluate IVF, including its emotional and physical stress, low success rates and the risk of multiple births, and it is regularly tested as a 4 to 6 mark evaluation or data question.

terms.d: A drug containing FSH and LH given to a woman whose own FSH level is too low to stimulate eggs to mature.
Follicle stimulating hormone, from the pituitary; causes maturation of an egg in the ovary.
Luteinising hormone, from the pituitary; stimulates the release of the egg.
Treatment in which eggs are fertilised by sperm in the laboratory and the embryos are inserted into the mother's uterus.
A fertilised egg that has begun to divide and develop into a tiny ball of cells.
The release of a mature egg from an ovary.
The womb, where an embryo implants and develops.
The tube along which the egg travels from the ovary to the uterus; the site of natural fertilisation.
The fusion of the nucleus of a sperm with the nucleus of an egg.
The attachment of an embryo to the lining of the uterus.
The birth of more than one baby from a pregnancy, e.g. twins, a risk of IVF.
The percentage of treatment cycles that result in a live birth.
A moral question on which people hold different views, e.g. what should happen to unused embryos.
The gland at the base of the brain that makes FSH and LH.

worked.ans: (a) 32% and 11%. (b) Success is much lower in older women (11% compared with 32%), probably because egg quality and number decrease with age.
worked.q:
A clinic reports the results of IVF for two groups of women.
Women under 35: 800 cycles, 256 live births.
Women aged 40 to 42: 500 cycles, 55 live births.
(a) Calculate the success rate for each group. (2)
(b) Describe and suggest a reason for the difference. (2)
steps: (b) The success rate is 21 percentage points lower in the older group (32 minus 11), about three times lower (32 ÷ 11 is about 2.9).
Suggest: egg quality and number fall with age, so embryos are less likely to implant.

worked.ans: Model answer: The mother is given FSH and LH to make several eggs mature. The eggs are collected and fertilised in the laboratory using the father's sperm. The fertilised eggs develop into embryos, and when they are tiny balls of cells one or two are inserted into the mother's uterus.
worked.q: Describe how IVF is carried out. (6 marks)
steps: The mother is given FSH and LH (1) to stimulate several eggs to mature (1).
The eggs are collected from the mother's ovaries (1).
They are fertilised with sperm from the father in the laboratory (1).
The fertilised eggs develop into embryos, tiny balls of cells (1).
One or two embryos are inserted into the mother's uterus (1).

worked.ans: Model answer: IVF gives a chance of a baby to couples who cannot conceive naturally. However it is emotionally and physically stressful, the success rate is not high, and multiple births are a health risk to the mother and babies. Overall it is worthwhile when other treatments have failed, provided the number of embryos is limited and couples understand the risks.
worked.q: Evaluate the use of IVF for couples who cannot conceive naturally. (4 marks)
steps: Advantage: gives couples who cannot conceive a chance of having a baby (1).
Disadvantage: emotionally and physically stressful, and success rates are not high (1).
Disadvantage: may lead to multiple births, a risk to the babies and mother (1).
Conclusion with justification, e.g. worthwhile for couples with no other option if risks are explained (1).
